text: You're given an integer array called nums. You start at index zero. Each value, nums at i, is the maximum forward jump from index i. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index. You can assume the last index is always reachable.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — from index i, I can land anywhere from i plus one, up to i plus nums at i. Forward only. I return a count, not the path. And since the end is always reachable, I never need to return minus one. Is that right?
Yes. Just the count, and you can trust the guarantee.

Okay. One fact from Jump Game one helps a lot here. If I can reach index j, I can reach every index before j too, because the jump could just stop shorter. So, the cells I can reach is always a prefix, not a random set. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The length is between one and ten to the fourth, and every value is between zero and one thousand.

Got it. n can be one. Then I'm already on the last index, so the answer is zero. The answer is at most n minus one, when every step is a jump of one. And the biggest sum I compute is i plus nums at i, which is at most ninety-nine ninety-eight plus one thousand — ten thousand nine hundred ninety-eight. That fits easily in an int. Let me run through the example. Two, three, one, one, four. With zero jumps I'm at index zero. With one jump I can be at index one or two. From index one I can jump three, straight to index four. So the answer is two. The second example, two, three, zero, one, four, is also two, by the same path — zero, one, four. The zero at index two doesn't matter, because I never need to stand there.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to use dynamic programming. D P at j is the fewest jumps to reach j. For each i, I try every j it can reach, and take the minimum of D P at j, and D P at i plus one. That's correct, but it's order n times the max jump. Up to about ten to the seventh steps here. I'd keep it as a checker, not the answer. This problem reminds me of B F S shortest path. Fewest jumps is fewest edges, and every edge costs one. So I can think in layers. Layer k is the set of cells I can reach in exactly k jumps, and not fewer. The answer is the layer number of the last index. And now the prefix fact pays off. Reachable within k jumps is a prefix. So each layer is a contiguous range — it starts right after the last layer ends. That means I don't need a queue. A layer is just a right edge. For example one, layer zero is index zero alone. Layer one is indices one through two. Layer two is indices three through four. Index four is in layer two, so the answer is two. My job is just to find where each layer ends, while scanning left to right.

Here's the plan. It's B F S, but with two numbers instead of a queue. I keep two edges. Cur-end is the right edge of the layer I can reach with the current number of jumps. Next-end is the farthest index reachable with one more jump, from any cell scanned so far. Both start at zero, and so does the step counter. Then I scan i from zero up to n minus two — standing on the last index needs no jump. At each cell, next-end becomes the max of itself and i plus nums at i — cell i grows the next layer. And if i has reached cur-end, the current layer is fully scanned, so I must take one more jump: step goes up by one, and cur-end moves to next-end. At the end I return step. So here, I'm using cur-end to keep track of where the current layer stops, and next-end collects, from every cell in the current layer, how far one more jump could go. When i reaches cur-end, I've seen every cell of the current layer. The next layer can't grow anymore. So I close it. The key idea: this code never decides which cell to jump from. It only tracks how far each layer goes. The real path is hidden inside the layers, and I don't need it, because the question only asks for the count. One thing worth flagging — the loop stops at n minus two, not n minus one. Index n minus one is always the edge of the last layer, because nothing past it exists. If I scanned it, the cur-end check would fire one extra time, and add one for a jump I never take. That version is always exactly one too high. Even a single-element array gives one instead of zero. There's a trade-off here. I could also write a plain B F S with a queue, or keep explicit left and right bounds per layer. Same linear time, same answers, but more code and more state. The two-number version is shorter, and it's constant space. So I'll go with that. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. I write a function called jump that takes the array. Three ints, all starting at zero: step, cur-end, and next-end. Then a for loop, i from zero, while i is less than the size minus one. Inside, next-end becomes the max of next-end, and i plus nums at i. Then, if cur-end equals i, I increment step, and set cur-end to next-end. After the loop, I return step. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — the order inside the loop matters. I update next-end before the cur-end check. Cell i is part of the layer I'm closing, so its reach must count before I close it. If I swap the two lines, then at i equals zero, next-end is still zero. The first layer closes with edge zero, and things go wrong from there. Example one returns one instead of two. Also, compiling with all warnings on gives one sign-compare warning, because int i is compared against size, which is unsigned. It's harmless here, since n is at least one. For n equals one, size minus one is zero, and the loop doesn't run. Only an empty vector would wrap around to a huge number, and that's outside the constraints. Writing int n equals the size first, and comparing i against n minus one, removes the warning and gives the same answers.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Example one: two, three, one, one, four. Expected output is two. n is five, so i goes from zero to three. At i equals zero, the value is two, so next-end becomes two. And i equals cur-end, so layer zero is done — step becomes one, cur-end becomes two. At i equals one, the three pushes next-end to four. But i is not cur-end yet, so I don't jump — layer one isn't fully scanned. At i equals two, next-end stays at four, and I hit cur-end. Layer one is done, so step becomes two, and cur-end moves to four. At i equals three, nothing changes. Then the loop ends — i equals four is the last index, and it's not scanned. I return two. That matches. Example two gives the exact same table, except at i equals two the sum is two plus zero, which is two. That zero does nothing, because next-end is already four. Now the case that shows why I never pick a cell: four, one, one, three, one, one, one. The answer is two. Layer zero is index zero. Layer one is indices one through four. While I scan it, i equals three pushes next-end to three plus three, which is six — the last index. Then at i equals four, layer one closes and step becomes two. The best path is zero, three, six, and index three is in the middle of layer one. A greedy that always jumps as far as possible goes zero, four, five, six. That's three jumps, which is wrong. Jumping far now can leave you on a weak cell. Scanning the whole layer avoids that choice. Let's also test with corner cases. A single zero gives zero — the loop runs zero times. Four ones gives three — every i is a layer end, each layer is one cell. Three, zero, zero, one gives one — one jump covers everything, the zeros never matter. One, two, one, one, one gives three. And at the top of the constraints, ten thousand ones gives nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine, the worst case. All one-thousands gives ten. And one thousand followed by all ones gives nine thousand: one big jump to index one thousand, then eight thousand nine hundred ninety-nine single steps.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is linear. One pass over indices zero to n minus two, with one max and one compare each. The space complexity is constant. Three integers. In the worst-case scenario the loop always runs n minus one times. There's no early exit. For ten thousand elements that's about six and a half microseconds. The largest next-end is ten thousand nine hundred ninety-eight, so an int is safe. I'd test this against a B F S checker. Every array of length one to eight, with values zero to three, that can reach the end — that's forty-one thousand six hundred arrays. Plus random ones, up to two thousand elements with values up to one thousand. Two hundred sixty-one thousand six hundred cases total, zero mismatches. The same test shows how the bugs fail. Scanning the last index fails about twenty-one thousand cases, always exactly one too high. Checking before updating fails over forty-one thousand. And one trap: counting a jump every time next-end improves fails over twenty-three thousand cases, but it passes both official examples. The smallest failure is two, two, zero: it says two, and the right answer is one. Always jumping the full distance fails almost twelve thousand, and it loops forever on a zero. Oh, one more thing — this code trusts the guarantee. It never returns minus one. If the end were not reachable, it would still return a normal-looking number. Three, two, one, zero, four returns two, even though index four can't be reached. If the guarantee could break, I'd add the Jump Game one check: if next-end is still stuck at i when a layer closes, return minus one.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You framed it as a B F S by layers, and used the prefix fact to show each layer is a range, so cur-end and next-end replace the queue. You showed with four, one, one, three, one, one, one why the code must not pick a jump: the best jump comes from the middle of a layer, and jump-farthest takes three. And you nailed the two order details — stopping at n minus two, and updating before the check — plus the trap that passes both examples but fails two, two, zero. Good work.
